title: The Fall of Samaria and Why It Happened
summary: Hoshea, Israel's last king, rebels against Assyria by seeking help from Egypt; the Assyrians imprison him, besiege Samaria for three years, capture it, and deport the Israelites to distant parts of their empire. The narrator then stops the story to explain the disaster: Israel worshiped other gods, ignored the prophets, and rejected the covenant. The chapter ends with foreign peoples resettled in the land, who worship the LORD alongside their own gods.
story: This is the end of the northern kingdom. Since Jeroboam son of Nebat set up the golden calves (1 Kings 12), about two centuries earlier, every northern king has been judged for walking in his sins, and chapter after chapter has warned where it would lead. Now it arrives. The ten tribes that broke from David's house are carried off and never return as a kingdom. The narrator gives the event only six verses and then spends thirty-five explaining it, because what the reader most needs is not the details of the siege but the reasons. Verses 18-20 also turn the warning toward Judah, which has begun walking in Israel's customs. The rest of 2 Kings asks whether Judah will learn from Samaria's fall; the answer comes in chapter 25.
historical:
Hoshea reigned from about 732 to 722 BC. He came to power as an Assyrian vassal, but after Tiglath-pileser III died in 727 BC he withheld tribute and turned to Egypt. The identity of King So is debated: some scholars identify him with Osorkon IV, a pharaoh of the late eighth century, while others think the Hebrew originally referred to the Egyptian city of Sais rather than a king's name. Egypt was divided among rival rulers at the time and sent no help.

Shalmaneser V (727-722 BC) besieged Samaria, and the city fell in 722 BC. Shalmaneser died about the same time, and his successor Sargon II claimed the conquest in his own inscriptions, reporting that he deported about 27,000 people and resettled the city with captives from other lands. The places named in verse 6 were in northern Mesopotamia (Halah, and Gozan on the Habor River) and in Media, in what is now northwestern Iran. The peoples brought into Samaria (verse 24) came from Babylonia and Syria, and Assyrian records confirm that such population exchanges were standard imperial policy, designed to break local loyalties.
cultural:
Ancient peoples commonly believed that each land had its own god, who had to be honored by whoever lived there. The resettled foreigners in verses 25-28 think exactly this way: the lions mean they don't know the requirements of the god of the land, so a priest must teach them. The Assyrian king agrees and sends back an Israelite priest, who teaches at Bethel, the old shrine of Jeroboam's calf. The result is a mixed religion in which the LORD is added to each group's existing gods. Several of those gods are known from Mesopotamian sources, such as Nergal, the god of the underworld worshiped at Cuthah.

The long list of sins in verses 7-17 describes practices common across Canaan: high places, standing stones (sacred pillars, upright stones marking a god's presence), wooden Asherah poles for the goddess Asherah, worship of the sun, moon, and stars (the host of heaven), divination, and child sacrifice. For Israel each of these was a breach of the covenant made at Sinai, the binding relationship in which the LORD had promised to be their God and they had promised to worship him alone. The sermon in verses 35-39 echoes the first commandment and the language of Deuteronomy almost phrase by phrase.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-6 are a spare report in the usual regnal style, with no drama and no speeches. Verses 7-23 are a sermon by the narrator, one of the most important interpretive passages in the Old Testament, in which the history of Israel from the exodus to the exile is summed up as a history of unfaithfulness. It is built with the vocabulary of Deuteronomy: statutes, commandments, covenant, provoking the LORD, stiffening the neck, the prophets as his servants. Verses 24-41 describe the new population, and they are framed by the key verb of the section, to fear (the BSB renders it "worship"): they feared the LORD and served their own gods. The repeated phrase "to this day" (verses 23, 34, 41) addresses the book's first readers directly, as people living with the consequences.

doctrines.note: Samaria's fall is explained as the LORD's judgment, not simply Assyria's victory. God is patient for generations, warning through prophets, but his patience has an end, and the covenant's curses (Deuteronomy 28) come true in history.
The chapter treats idolatry as the root sin that produces the others. Verse 15 gives its logic: those who pursue worthless things become worthless themselves. People become like what they worship.
Verse 13 says the LORD warned Israel and Judah through all his prophets and seers. The exile did not come without warning; the sin was not ignorance but refusal to listen.

The key terms of the sermon are covenant words: statutes, commandments, the covenant made with their fathers. Israel's relationship with God was a covenant with promises and obligations, and the chapter measures the nation against it.

words.note: Hevel, breath or vapor, and so what is empty or worthless. Verse 15 pairs the noun with its related verb in a pun: they went after hevel and themselves became hevel. The same word is the refrain of Ecclesiastes (usually translated vanity or meaningless), and Jeremiah 2:5 uses the same wordplay. Idols have no substance, and those who trust them lose theirs.

Yare, to fear. In the Old Testament, to fear the LORD means to revere, worship, and obey him, and it is the heart of true religion. In verses 25-41 the settlers fear the LORD, which the BSB renders as worship, but they serve their own gods too. The narrator then says in verse 34 that they did not truly fear him. Reverence that is only one loyalty among many is not the fear of the LORD at all.

Ud, to warn or testify. It is a legal word, used of witnesses who bear testimony, and in verses 13 and 15 it describes the LORD solemnly warning Israel through the prophets. The prophets were witnesses in God's covenant lawsuit, and the exile is the verdict.

christ: The chapter's connection to Christ runs through its aftermath. The mixed population of the former northern kingdom became the ancestors, at least in part, of the Samaritans of the New Testament, whom many Jews of Jesus' day regarded as outsiders because of this history. Jesus deliberately crossed that divide. He spoke with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well and told her that the time was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4), made a Samaritan the hero of a parable (Luke 10), and sent his disciples to Samaria after his resurrection (Acts 1:8). Acts 8 describes Samaritans receiving the gospel. The chapter also shows the need that Christ meets: a people who could not keep the covenant despite every warning, waiting for the new covenant promised through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31-34), which the New Testament says Jesus established in his blood.

hard.q: Is this chapter a fair account of the Samaritans' origins?
hard.a:
Verses 24-41 describe the religion of foreign settlers in Samaria in the generations after 722 BC, and later Jewish writers often used this passage to portray the Samaritans as a mixed people with a false religion. The Samaritans told the story differently, seeing themselves as descendants of Israelites who had never left and as keepers of the true worship of the LORD on Mount Gerizim. Modern historians generally think both elements are real: Assyrian sources confirm large deportations and resettlement, but also show that many Israelites, especially in the countryside, stayed in the land.

The chapter is not written as an ethnic history. Its concern is theological: a people who add the LORD to their other gods have not understood who he is. It is also worth noticing that the narrator's harshest words in the chapter are aimed at Israel, and then at Judah, not at the foreigners. By the time of Jesus the Samaritans worshiped the LORD alone and kept the five books of Moses, and the New Testament treats them as people to whom the gospel belongs.

questions: Verse 15 says Israel pursued worthless idols and became worthless. In what ways do people become like the things they give their lives to?
The settlers worshiped the LORD but also served their own gods. What might it look like for faith today to be one loyalty among many rather than the one that orders the rest?
Israel had generations of warnings before the end came. How do you hear the patience of God: as permission to delay or as a call to turn?
